title: Order API timeouts overnight
executive_summary:
INC-004 (SEV2, order-service): order creation latency and intermittent timeouts occurred from about 02:15Z on 2026-09-11. Final status is ROOT_CAUSE_IDENTIFIED. The leading hypothesis (H1, confidence 0.8, status supported) is resource saturation in order-service: an invoice-reconciliation batch (batch_size=500000) started on node order-7f9c at 02:05Z (logpat-order-service-f3a6bc4b). This was followed by CPU rising to 70-100% from 02:08Z (met-order-service-cpu_pct-0145-0330), G1 GC pauses up to 8140 ms from 02:08:13Z (logpat-order-service-7b888968), order-worker pool saturation (active=200, queue up to 19250) from 02:12:03Z (logpat-order-service-300bdd51), and deadline errors from 02:15:11Z (logpat-order-service-1c82530b). Timeout rate rose from a baseline of 0.1% to a window maximum of about 6.4% (met-order-service-timeout_rate-0145-0330). Request rate was flat (met-order-service-request_rate-0145-0330), so traffic load is not the cause. The batch-to-symptom sequence is consistent in timing, but the batch's direct causal role is inferred from timing and co-location rather than batch-specific telemetry.

Alternative hypotheses were rejected. H2 (postgres report_rollup degradation) is contradicted by flat postgres p99 latency and flat DB connection utilisation on both postgres and order-service (met-postgres-p99_latency_ms-0145-0240, met-order-service-db_conn_util_pct-0145-0330), and by a postgres CPU rise that starts after the order-service GC onset. H3 (payment-service 5.7.3 deploy) is contradicted by flat payment p99 and timeout rate (met-payment-service-p99_latency_ms-2145-0240, met-payment-service-timeout_rate-0145-0240).

critic_review.summary: H1 (order-service resource saturation from the invoice-reconciliation batch on order-7f9c) is the leading hypothesis and is supported. Timing is consistent: batch start 02:05:00Z precedes CPU onset (02:08Z), the first GC pause (02:08:13Z, 8140 ms), pool saturation (02:12:03Z), memory rise (02:14-02:15Z) and deadline errors and timeout onset (02:15Z). Error rate rises from 0.54% to about 4% over the same window. Traffic is flat (request_rate +0.1%), so load is not the cause. Downstream payment latency and timeouts are flat, so the latency originates inside order-service. H2 (postgres report_rollup) is contradicted: postgres p99 is flat (25.06 vs 24.92 ms), DB connection utilisation is flat on both postgres and order-service, and the postgres CPU rise is small (35% to 44%) and starts after the order-service GC onset. H3 (payment 5.7.3 deploy) is contradicted: payment p99 and timeout rate are flat through the deploy and the onset, and the deploy is about 4h before onset with no mechanism evidence. Caveats: the batch is linked to the GC and CPU only by timing and co-location, with no batch-specific metric or thread dump; the CPU and GC metrics are service-level, so the claim that only order-7f9c is affected is unverified (per-node metrics are not exposed by the tools); and the inventory-reservation retries from 01:31Z are an unexplained low-level precursor that could be an early sign of the same contention. None of these overturn the category or culprit.

assessments.reasoning: Batch start precedes all anomalies. CPU onset, GC pauses, pool saturation, memory rise and timeout onset follow in the expected order. Payment latency is flat, so the latency is internal to order-service. Traffic is flat. Remaining gaps (per-node attribution, batch-specific resource profile) are limitations, not contradictions.

Postgres p99 and connection utilisation are flat, which contradicts DB-capacity degradation. The postgres CPU rise is modest and begins after the order-service GC onset. The slow report_rollup statements began at 01:47Z with no matching latency change, so they do not explain the 02:08Z onset.

Payment p99 latency and timeout rate are flat through the 22:15Z deploy and the 02:15Z onset. There is no order-service-to-payment latency change. The deploy is the only change in 24h, which is a temporal correlation only, and the order-service GC onset is ~4h later.

probable_root_cause.description: Invoice-reconciliation batch (batch_size=500000) started on node order-7f9c at 02:05Z exhausted CPU/heap in order-service, causing G1 GC pauses and order-worker pool saturation, which produced deadline timeouts and errors.
probable_root_cause.label: ROOT CAUSE IDENTIFIED (critic-approved; still an INFERENCE from evidence)

root_cause_statement: ROOT CAUSE IDENTIFIED (critic-approved; still an INFERENCE from evidence): resource_saturation in order-service - Invoice-reconciliation batch (batch_size=500000) started on node order-7f9c at 02:05Z exhausted CPU/heap in order-service, causing G1 GC pauses and order-worker pool saturation, which produced deadline timeouts and errors.
corrective_actions: Pause or throttle the invoice-reconciliation batch (batch_size=500000) on order-7f9c so the order-service CPU and heap pressure recedes; confirm it is not still running (no end-time evidence is currently available).
Drain or restart order-service instances on order-7f9c to clear the saturated order-worker pool (active=200, large queue) and confirm timeout and error rates return to baseline (about 0.1% timeouts).
Verify whether other order-service nodes are affected, since per-node metrics were not available and the affected-node scope is unverified.
Investigate the inventory-reservation retries first seen around 01:31Z (alternative explanation) to determine whether they were an early precursor of the same contention.
preventive_actions: Isolate batch workloads from request-serving order-service capacity (separate node pool, CPU and memory limits, or a dedicated worker), so batch execution cannot starve the order-worker pool.
Set the batch to process in smaller chunks with backpressure and checkpointing rather than a single batch_size=500000 run.
Review G1 GC tuning and heap sizing for order-service under batch load, and set bounded queue sizes with load shedding so the queue cannot reach about 19,250 entries.
Add batch-specific metrics (progress, duration, resource use per job) and emit a thread dump on pool saturation to strengthen causal attribution in future incidents.
monitoring_recommendations: Alert on order-service GC pause duration above, for example, 1000 ms and on sustained CPU above 80% per node, using per-node rather than service-level metrics.
Alert on order-worker pool active threads at or near the maximum and on queue depth above a defined threshold, with a leading indicator at the first GC pause.
Alert on POST /v1/orders deadline-exceeded errors and timeout rate above baseline (for example, above 1%), and monitor error rate.
Log the start and end of scheduled jobs with node and resource metadata, and track the invoice-reconciliation job's runtime and status.
Monitor postgres report_rollup() statement duration (alert above a few seconds) to keep rejecting H2 or detect it if it recurs.
Fix the metric query configuration so api-gateway and order-service queries stay within the 6-metric limit, so that the full evidence set (including db_conn_util_pct and error_rate) can be collected.
limitations: The batch is linked to the GC and CPU rise by timing and co-location only; no batch-specific metric or thread dump was available.
CPU, memory, and GC metrics are service-level, so the claim that only order-7f9c is affected is unverified.
No end-time or progress evidence exists for the batch, so whether it is still running is unknown.
Some metric queries failed due to the six-metric limit (api-gateway and order-service), so parts of the evidence set are incomplete.
Inventory-reservation retries from about 01:31Z are unexplained and may be an earlier precursor of the same contention.
2 tool calls failed and 0 returned partial data; affected areas are treated as unknown, not healthy.
Confidence values are rule-based evidence-strength scores, not calibrated probabilities.
Investigation terminated because: critic verdict APPROVED
conclusion: The most probable root cause is resource saturation in order-service caused by the invoice-reconciliation batch (batch_size=500000) on node order-7f9c, which led to GC pauses, worker-pool exhaustion, and deadline timeouts from 02:15Z. The conclusion is supported by timing, co-location, and the rejection of the postgres and payment-service alternatives. It is not fully confirmed: batch-specific telemetry, per-node metrics, and an explanation for the 01:31Z inventory-reservation retries are still missing. Mitigation should stop or throttle the batch, and preventive work should isolate batch workloads from order-serving capacity.
